purpose: Survey of language implementations that can run inside a browser WASM engine, modelled as an optional compiler module (source S -> interpreter module) plus an interpreter module (args [+ S] -> result). Scored for portability onto the Scaffold contract ABI.

scaffoldContext.contractAbi: Guest exports `alloc` and `run`; imports `scaffold_env.{contract_hash,params,claim,get_result,set_result,debug,reject}` plus `scaffold_walker.*` / `scaffold_builder.*`. No filesystem, no clock, no randomness, no argv. Blocking host calls are supported via JSPI (src/contract/wasm/JspiTransport.ts) or a sync in-process transport.
scaffoldContext.determinismTransformer: scripts/wasm-determinism rewrites/validates modules. BANNED: atomics + shared memory, all SIMD arithmetic/lane ops (0xfd family, minus byte-level v128 load/store), WasmGC (0xfb family), exception handling (try_table/throw/throw_ref/legacy try-catch), the reinterpret family (f32.reinterpret_i32 etc.). REWRITTEN: own memory section -> import of env.memory; memory.grow/table.grow get an abstain guard; NaN canonicalized before f32/f64 store and copysign.
scaffoldContext.practicalConsequence: WasmGC and Wasm exception-handling backends are hard-blocked today. SIMD and threads require a rebuild with those features off. Plain scalar C/Zig/Rust compiled to wasm32 is the sweet spot.

fieldGuide.language: The source language S that this implementation lets you run.
fieldGuide.compiler: The stage that consumes source S. null when the implementation interprets S directly. `hostedInWasm: false` means the compiler exists but only runs natively (so S must be compiled off-chain).
fieldGuide.interpreter: The stage that actually executes. For AOT toolchains this is the emitted module itself.
fieldGuide.hostBindings: wasi-p1 | wasi-p2 | wasix | emscripten-js (needs generated JS glue) | custom (module-specific import table) | none (pure wasm, no imports beyond memory).
fieldGuide.howToGetWasm: prebuilt (a published .wasm you can download today) | buildable (upstream supports a wasm build you run yourself) | plausible (no wasm build upstream, but no fundamental blocker) | native-only.
fieldGuide.rebuildForScaffold.difficulty: easy | moderate | hard | blocked -- how much work to re-target imports/exports at the Scaffold ABI.
fieldGuide.determinism.verdict: ok | needs-rebuild | likely-blocked | blocked -- against the rules in scaffoldContext.determinismTransformer.
fieldGuide.confidence: verified-local (inspected artifacts on this machine) | documented (primary project docs/releases) | reported (secondary sources) | uncertain.

implementations.name: Zig compiler, self-hosted wasm backend (zig-wasm-zig2wasm.wasm)

compiler.buildRecipe: build_wasm_zig2wasm.sh: bootstrap zig1 -> zig2 (native, -ofmt=c), cross-compile the compiler to C for wasm32-wasi with dev=.wasm, clang --target=wasm32-wasip1 + wasi-libc, then rewrite `env.*` imports to `wasi_snapshot_preview1.*` via wasm2wat/wat2wasm. Needs two source patches (src/dev.zig .legalize, src/main.zig self_exe_path on WASI), applied and reverted automatically.
compiler.sourceDelivery: WASI filesystem: --dir mounted source tree plus the zig std lib (--zig-lib-dir) and cache dirs
compiler.outputForm: wasm32-freestanding .wasm written to the WASI fs

interpreter.notes: Output is whatever the Zig program declares; the Scaffold determinism contracts are themselves built this way.

implementations.verifiedBehaviour: Build script step 5 runs the wasm compiler under wasmtime and compiles a Zig source file to wasm32-freestanding, i.e. Zig-to-WASM entirely inside WASM, no LLVM.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The compiler stage needs a real filesystem, so it needs a WASI-p1 shim over an in-memory VFS (source + ~40MB std lib + cache). Feasible but heavy for an on-chain compiler. The emitted modules are trivially Scaffold-shaped -- just export alloc/run and import scaffold_env.

determinism.notes: Compiler stage: must stub clock_time_get/random_get, and the compiler cache must be keyed deterministically. Output stage: ReleaseSmall Zig emits no SIMD/EH/GC, so emitted modules pass the transformer as-is.

implementations.sizeCaveat: 5.8MB module, and the std lib tree it needs dwarfs it.

compiler.buildRecipe: build_wasm_wasi.sh -- same bootstrap, but dev=.bootstrap, so the wasm-hosted compiler can only emit `-ofmt=c`.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Only useful chained with a C compiler; superseded by the zig2wasm build above. Listed because it is the simpler, more robust of the two builds.

determinism.notes: Same clock/random stubbing as above.

implementations.name: QuickJS-NG, official WASI build

compiler.artifact: qjs -c / qjsc bytecode compiler (also runs inside the same wasm module)
compiler.outputForm: QuickJS bytecode (C array or binary), consumed by the same engine
compiler.notes: Optional stage -- QuickJS also evals source directly.

interpreter.sourceDelivery: WASI fs / stdin / C API in reactor mode (create context, eval repeatedly)

implementations.releaseNote: qjs-wasi.wasm ~1.46MB and qjs-wasi-reactor.wasm ~1.45MB published as release artifacts (May 2026).

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Best-in-class candidate. Reactor mode is already the right shape: instantiate once, call an exported eval entry point. Only a handful of WASI calls are actually needed (fd_write for stdout, proc_exit, clock/random which you want stubbed anyway). Swapping those for scaffold_env is a small shim; a native build against wasi-libc with a custom import module is also straightforward.

determinism.notes: Plain C, no WasmGC, no Wasm EH, no SIMD in a default build. Main risk is the banned reinterpret family: number formatting/parsing (dtoa/strtod) and NaN-boxing bit-punch doubles. Needs an actual transformer run on the artifact to confirm; if it trips, a memcpy-based build usually avoids reinterpret.

interpreter.sourceDelivery: JS string passed through the generated glue

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The most ergonomic browser JS sandbox today, but the Emscripten glue is the API. For Scaffold you would rebuild the same C sources against wasi-sdk (see quickjs-ng-wasi) rather than port the glue. Asyncify variants also fight the determinism transformer's assumptions less than JSPI, but add size.

determinism.notes: Requires the JS side; not a standalone module.

implementations.name: Javy (dynamic linking mode)
implementations.architecturalNote: This is the closest existing thing to the compiler/interpreter split in the model: `javy build -C dynamic` emits a 1-16KB module containing only the user's bytecode, which imports two functions from a separately-deployed QuickJS provider module.

compiler.hostBindings: n/a (native CLI; internally runs QuickJS under Wasmtime + Wizer)
compiler.outputForm: wasm module holding QuickJS bytecode, importing javy_quickjs_provider_v1
compiler.notes: The compiler is a native binary today, but its engine is QuickJS-in-wasm plus Wizer, so a wasm-hosted version is not far-fetched.

interpreter.pluginAbi: realloc(old_ptr, old_size, align, new_size) and eval_bytecode(ptr, size)
interpreter.notes: Static mode instead inlines the engine: >=869KB per module. Dynamic mode: 1-16KB per module against one shared 869KB interpreter.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Strongest structural fit in the whole dataset. One interpreter module deployed once as a Scaffold contract; each 'program' is a few KB of bytecode that can live in a block. The two-function plugin ABI is trivially expressible in the Scaffold ABI. Version pinning between bytecode and plugin is explicit, which suits content-addressed deployment.

determinism.notes: Same QuickJS caveats as quickjs-ng-wasi.

compiler.sourceDelivery: JS source evaluated into a live VM, then snapshotted
compiler.outputForm: a serialized VM state (including pending promises) restorable into a fresh instance
compiler.notes: Snapshot-as-compiler: source in, resumable interpreter state out.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Interesting for long-running/resumable executions across blocks: a snapshot is a deterministic, content-addressable continuation. One VM per instance (no shared memory between contexts) matches Scaffold isolation.

determinism.notes: Snapshot format must be byte-deterministic to be usable as protocol state.

compiler.artifact: porffor CLI (written in JS, so it runs in a browser as JS -- not itself a wasm module)

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The only true AOT JS->wasm compiler. Output is reportedly 10-30x smaller/faster than interpreter-bundling approaches, which matters enormously if every program is a separate on-chain module. The catch is language coverage: it is a research project and does not implement all of JS.

determinism.notes: Output is plain scalar wasm; likely the cleanest determinism story for JS if the subset is enough.

compiler.artifact: componentize-js (bundles JS + SpiderMonkey into a WASI-p2 component, Wizer-preinitialized)

interpreter.notes: Runs in browsers only after `jco transpile` back to core wasm + JS glue.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Full-fat engine (tens of MB), component-model-shaped, and browsers have no native component support -- you would transpile through jco, reintroducing JS glue. Worth knowing about for spec completeness, not a near-term Scaffold candidate.

determinism.notes: SpiderMonkey's wasm build uses features the transformer bans; a stripped rebuild is a large project.

implementations.name: Pyodide (CPython + Emscripten)

interpreter.sourceDelivery: Python source string via runPython(), or a package/wheel loaded into the Emscripten VFS

implementations.versionNote: Versioning now tracks CPython (Pyodide 314.x = CPython 3.14). Packages can publish WebAssembly wheels to PyPI, so C/Rust extensions load as .wasm in the browser.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Deeply Emscripten-coupled: the JS glue implements the filesystem, the JS<->Python object bridge, and dynamic linking of extension wheels. Porting to a bare scaffold_env import table means giving all of that up. Use MicroPython or Monty instead if you want Python-shaped semantics under a tight ABI.

determinism.notes: Also large enough that per-execution instantiation cost is a real problem.

compiler.notes: Small C program; a wasm build of mpy-cross would give a clean compiler/interpreter split like Javy's.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: ~303KB base and millisecond startup make this the most realistic Python for a per-execution model. The upstream port is Emscripten-based, but MicroPython is designed to be embedded against arbitrary host hooks, so a wasm32-freestanding build against scaffold_env is a well-trodden kind of port.

determinism.notes: MicroPython's NLR (exception) mechanism uses setjmp/longjmp; on Emscripten that can lower to Wasm EH, which the transformer bans. Check which NLR backend the build selects.

interpreter.artifact: standalone wasm build (also ships as a Pyodide wheel)

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Written in Rust and designed exactly for the constraints Scaffold has: microsecond startup, no filesystem/network/env access, only explicit developer-provided host calls, hard limits on memory and CPU. Released Feb 2026, so young, and it is a Python-like subset rather than Python.

determinism.notes: Rust->wasm32 with no ambient capability surface; the deliberate host-call design maps onto scaffold_env almost directly.

interpreter.notes: wasm-bindgen glue by default; a wasm32-wasip1 build also exists.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Pure Rust, so retargeting imports is a Cargo feature/shim exercise rather than a C build-system fight. Larger and slower than MicroPython, less complete than CPython.

determinism.notes: Watch for SIMD in dependencies (hashbrown/ahash) -- build with target features off.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Component-model-first; browsers need jco transpilation. Same size problem as Pyodide.

interpreter.notes: Runs in-browser through @wasmer/sdk, which implements WASIX in JS.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: WASIX is a much larger host surface than WASI p1 (threads, sockets, posix_spawn). Shimming all of it over scaffold_env is not realistic; you would rebuild CPython against wasi-sdk instead.

compiler.outputForm: wasm module (direct WASM backend, no LLVM)
compiler.notes: Shares its ASR/backends with LFortran, including the fast direct-to-WASM backend.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Alpha-stage compiler, but the architecture -- compiler-in-wasm emitting plain scalar wasm without LLVM -- is exactly the shape you want.

determinism.notes: Direct WASM backend emits simple scalar code.

implementations.name: ruby.wasm (official CRuby port)

compiler.outputForm: a new self-contained .wasm with the files packed into a virtual filesystem baked into the module
compiler.notes: wasi-vfs is a genuine 'source in, interpreter out' compiler stage: it links a static VFS into the interpreter module without rebuilding Ruby.

interpreter.sourceDelivery: packed VFS, or eval via the JS bindings

implementations.statusNote: Actively maintained (@ruby/wasm-wasi 2.9.x as of mid-2026). No threads, no networking on the WASI target.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The wasi-vfs pattern is worth stealing regardless of language: it turns 'source S' into 'a content-addressed module that contains S'. Ruby itself is large and uses a conservative stack-scanning GC, which needs care under any custom host.

determinism.notes: Uses setjmp/longjmp and stack scanning; verify against the transformer. Size makes per-execution instantiation expensive.

implementations.name: php-wasm (WordPress Playground)

interpreter.sourceDelivery: writeFile() into the Emscripten VFS then run()
interpreter.notes: PHP extensions load as dynamic .so modules; the build feeds symbol references back to the linker as explicit exports.

implementations.statusNote: Jan 2026 package split moved binaries out of the main packages (npm 100MB limit); Mar 2026 build work cut 122MB of binary size.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: One of the most production-proven wasm language runtimes anywhere, but it is Emscripten to the core: dynamic .so loading, a JS-implemented filesystem, and a C API module designed around JS. Not a near-term ABI port.

compiler.artifact: luac (built into the Lua VM: string.dump / load)

interpreter.notes: No WASI bindings; the interop layer is JS.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Lua is the classic embeddable interpreter: ~250KB of ANSI C, a documented C API, and a built-in bytecode compiler you get for free. Building vanilla Lua against wasi-sdk or wasm32-freestanding with a scaffold_env import table is a weekend project, and load()/string.dump() gives you the compiler/interpreter split natively.

determinism.notes: Plain scalar C, no EH, no SIMD, no GC opcodes. Lua numbers are f64, so NaN canonicalization applies; and its bytecode format is version/platform-specific, so pin it. Probably the single easiest real language to get running under the Scaffold ABI.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Browser-only, no WASI implementation, low current activity.

interpreter.sourceDelivery: R expression string; packages from a wasm CRAN mirror

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Browser-only by design (Akamai's matrix lists R as browser-yes/WASI-no). Huge Fortran/C numerical core.

determinism.notes: Numerics-first language is the worst case for cross-engine float reproducibility even with NaN canonicalization.

implementations.name: SWI-Prolog WASM
implementations.statusNote: Officially supported by the standard build since 8.1.2; 2025 added engines for concurrent async Prolog tasks and a WASM shell debugger.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Interesting fit for a consensus system: declarative, deterministic query semantics, and a natural query/answer request-response shape. Emscripten-coupled today.

determinism.notes: Core WAM execution is deterministic given a fixed clause order.

compiler.artifact: lfortran compiled to wasm (dev.lfortran.org runs it in-browser)
compiler.outputForm: wasm module, via either the direct WASM backend (fast) or the LLVM backend
compiler.notes: One of very few compilers that both runs as wasm and emits wasm.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Architecturally ideal (compiler-in-wasm, no LLVM needed for the fast path); the language and the compiler's maturity are the limiting factors.

determinism.notes: Float-heavy language; NaN canonicalization and a no-SIMD build are mandatory.

compiler.artifact: clang + lld + system libraries, run via @wasmer/sdk
compiler.notes: Needs posix_spawn (clang driver forks lld), which is why it needs WASIX rather than WASI p1. Verified working in Chrome, Firefox and Safari.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: ~100MB uncompressed (target ~30MB compressed) and a process-spawning host surface. Realistic as a developer-side tool, not as an on-chain compiler contract.

determinism.notes: Emitted modules are fine; the compiler stage is the problem.

compiler.sourceDelivery: in-memory virtual filesystem implemented in JS

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Predates the WASIX approach and separates clang from lld explicitly, which avoids posix_spawn -- a useful reference if you ever want an in-protocol C compiler. Old and unmaintained.

implementations.name: TCC (Tiny C Compiler) compiled to WASM

compiler.artifact: tcc.wasm (built with the Zig compiler, wasm32-freestanding)
compiler.sourceDelivery: source bytes written into linear memory; a Zig wrapper emulates the ~72 POSIX functions TCC expects, including a minimal fake filesystem
compiler.outputForm: RISC-V ELF in that project; TCC has no wasm codegen backend

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The most interesting *shape* in the C world: a whole C compiler in a few hundred KB with a hand-written, auditable syscall shim -- exactly the kind of thing that could be a Scaffold contract. Blocked on codegen: TCC has no WebAssembly backend, so today it produces native code, not wasm. Adding one is a real but bounded project.

determinism.notes: Freestanding build with an explicit, tiny import surface -- nothing the transformer objects to.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Key operational fact for this whole survey: `-sSTANDALONE_WASM` (and plain `emcc -O3 x.c -o x.wasm`) emits a module that creates its own memory and uses WASI instead of JS glue -- but it is best-effort. If the program touches an API with no non-JS equivalent, JS glue comes back. Several projects have reported that STANDALONE_WASM/PURE_WASI are not fully honoured. Treat any 'just rebuild it standalone' plan as needing verification per project.

determinism.notes: Build with exceptions and SIMD off.

interpreter.artifact: emitted module (contains the Go runtime + GC + scheduler)

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Every Go binary carries the runtime, GC and goroutine scheduler. The scheduler wants to yield to the host, which is why Go wasm modules are awkward under a call-in/call-out ABI. Multi-MB minimum output.

determinism.notes: The GC and map iteration order are the classic nondeterminism traps; Go randomizes map iteration deliberately.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The `wasm-unknown` target emits a module with essentially no imports, and //export lets you name exports directly -- a Scaffold contract in Go is straightforward. Cost: no reflection-heavy libraries, limited goroutine support, subset stdlib.

determinism.notes: LLVM-based, scalar output with default flags; the conservative GC allocates from linear memory (watch memory.grow, which the transformer instruments).

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Proves the concept -- a Go interpreter running as wasm, so Go source is data rather than a build input -- but 38MB and WASI's single-shot command model make it impractical here.

compiler.notes: Long-standing internals discussion, no shipping wasm-hosted rustc. Blockers: LLVM size, process spawning for the linker, and the filesystem-heavy driver. Rust->wasm output is of course completely mature (wasm32-unknown-unknown, wasm32-wasip1/p2).

rebuildForScaffold.notes: For *writing* Scaffold contracts, Rust is a first-class option: #[no_std] + wasm32-unknown-unknown + extern "C" imports gives you exactly the scaffold_env shape. For running Rust *as data*, there is nothing.

determinism.notes: Disable SIMD-using dependencies; core/alloc are scalar.

interpreter.artifact: CheerpJ runtime (a full WebAssembly JVM with OpenJDK class library)
interpreter.sourceDelivery: .class/.jar bytecode at runtime -- no build step
interpreter.notes: Includes an emulation layer for filesystem, networking and other OS-level features. Java 17 targeted for CheerpJ 5.0, LTS parity aimed at end of 2026.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Conceptually the purest 'interpreter takes source S as data' entry for a mainstream language -- you hand it a jar. But it is proprietary, browser-coupled, and enormous.

determinism.notes: JIT-generating wasm at runtime is fundamentally at odds with a pre-validated deterministic module.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Output is WasmGC.

determinism.notes: The determinism transformer bans the entire 0xfb GC opcode family. The deeper objection is that delegating to the host GC moves the allocator out of the hashed module and into the engine, where it cannot be audited or version-pinned. See scripts/wasm-determinism/README.md.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: WasmGC-only for the browser target.

determinism.notes: WasmGC has been baseline across Chrome 119 / Firefox 120 / Safari 18.2 since late 2024, and Wasm 3.0 standardized it in Sept 2025 -- so this is a Scaffold policy constraint, not a browser one.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: WasmGC only.

determinism.notes: Production-recommended since Flutter 3.22.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Stable since Scala.js 1.22.0, but uses both banned feature families.

compiler.artifact: Roslyn (native/JVM-free but not wasm-hosted); optional AOT step compiles IL to wasm

interpreter.artifact: dotnet.wasm (Mono runtime compiled to wasm; loads and interprets .NET assemblies)
interpreter.notes: Genuine two-stage model: the wasm module is the runtime, the assemblies are the program. AOT mode instead compiles IL to wasm ahead of time for ~95% of native speed at much larger size.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Structurally attractive (ship IL, not wasm), practically Emscripten-bound and very large.

determinism.notes: .NET leans on exceptions pervasively.

implementations.name: Swift SDK for WebAssembly

compiler.artifact: swiftc with the Wasm SDK (native-hosted); an Emscripten-hosted Swift toolchain is in development as of July 2026

interpreter.notes: Embedded Swift mode produces much smaller binaries and is supported in the distributed SDK bundles.

implementations.statusNote: Officially supported since Swift 6.2 (SDKs on swift.org); 6.3 SDKs shipping. WasmKit is a Swift-native wasm runtime that `swift run` can delegate to.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Embedded Swift + wasm32 with a hand-written import table is plausible; ARC means no GC opcodes, which is a real advantage over the WasmGC languages here.

determinism.notes: Standard Swift uses error handling that lowers to returns, not Wasm EH -- worth confirming per build.

implementations.name: GHC WebAssembly backend

interpreter.hostBindings: wasi-p1 (+ optional JavaScript FFI in browsers)
interpreter.notes: The JSFFI lets Haskell values reference JS values as first-class GC'd heap objects and lets one Haskell thread block on a JS promise without blocking the runtime.

implementations.statusNote: Supported from GHC 9.10 onward; documented in the official user's guide through 9.14/9.15.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Emits real WASI p1 modules with GHC's own GC in linear memory (no WasmGC), which is exactly the right property. Modules are large and the RTS does its own memory management, so the memory.grow abstain guard matters.

determinism.notes: GHC RTS is deterministic single-threaded; confirm no SIMD in the emitted primops.

implementations.name: wasm_of_ocaml
implementations.statusNote: First release Feb 2025; now the recommended OCaml wasm path, compatible with js_of_ocaml bindings and OCaml 5.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: WasmGC. js_of_ocaml (JS output) remains the alternative but is not wasm at all.

compiler.artifact: Hoot compiler + a self-contained WebAssembly toolchain written in Scheme
compiler.notes: Hoot ships its own assembler/linker in Scheme, so the compiler can itself be compiled to wasm and run in the browser -- a genuine compiler-in-wasm.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Output requires WasmGC and tail calls.

determinism.notes: The compiler-in-wasm architecture is worth studying even though the output format is currently unusable here.

compiler.artifact: elixirc -- and Popcorn can also compile Elixir client-side
compiler.outputForm: BEAM bytecode (.beam), which AtomVM then runs

interpreter.notes: The full BEAM was not feasible on wasm; AtomVM is a much smaller Erlang VM originally for microcontrollers.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Clean two-stage model (bytecode as data, small VM as the module) and AtomVM is explicitly designed for restricted environments. Real limitation is that AtomVM implements only a subset of Erlang/Elixir with custom, limited standard libraries. Process isolation and message-passing map unusually well onto a consensus system.

determinism.notes: Scheduler ordering must be pinned.

compiler.artifact: the official Gleam compiler compiled to wasm
compiler.sourceDelivery: source strings via a JS API
compiler.notes: Powers the official Gleam Playground and LiveCodes. Rust compiler, so the wasm build is a cargo target.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Excellent example of 'ship your compiler as a wasm module' for a Rust-written compiler, but its output targets JS/BEAM, so it does not close the loop to a wasm interpreter.

compiler.artifact: asc -- the compiler is itself written in AssemblyScript/TypeScript and is explicitly 'portable code'; it can be run in the browser for live hot-swapping of modules
compiler.sourceDelivery: source strings via the programmatic API

interpreter.notes: Emitted modules declare their own imports; you choose them.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Probably the shortest path to a working compiler-contract prototype: the compiler runs in the browser today, the language is TypeScript-shaped (which suits a TS codebase), output has a minimal runtime, and you declare the import table yourself so `scaffold_env` bindings are a one-liner. Caveat: AssemblyScript is not TypeScript -- no `any`, no closures over dynamic types, managed via its own linear-memory GC.

determinism.notes: Emits scalar wasm by default; its runtime (incremental GC) lives in linear memory, no WasmGC opcodes.

compiler.artifact: grain compiler (OCaml/Reason, distributed as a native binary or a JS bundle)

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Designed wasm-first (its runtime is in linear memory, no WasmGC), still pre-1.0. Active in 2026 (wit-bindgen work in April).

compiler.artifact: moonc (also runs in their container-free, offline-capable browser IDE)

interpreter.notes: Reported to produce smaller binaries than equivalent Rust or Go wasm, with sub-millisecond cold starts.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Wasm-native by design with a compiler that already runs in the browser -- structurally the closest thing to a purpose-built option. Downsides: beta, small ecosystem, and the toolchain's licensing/governance is not fully open in the way the others here are. Verify before betting on it.

determinism.notes: Has a WasmGC output mode as well as a linear-memory one -- pick the latter.

compiler.artifact: moc (OCaml); a wasm build backs the Motoko Playground

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The only language here designed from scratch for deterministic replicated execution on a blockchain: orthogonal persistence, an actor model, and a system-API import table conceptually parallel to scaffold_env. Closest prior art for what Scaffold contracts want, even if you never use it.

determinism.notes: The IC already enforces determinism constraints similar to Scaffold's; its rules are worth reading alongside scripts/wasm-determinism.

implementations.name: SQLite official WASM build
implementations.modelFit: The clean two-stage case: a DDL/INSERT stream is the 'compiler' input producing a database image; SELECTs are the 'interpreter' input against that image.

compiler.artifact: the same sqlite3.wasm, run in write mode
compiler.hostBindings: emscripten-js (default) | none (the core is plain C and builds freestanding)
compiler.outputForm: a database file image (deterministic bytes for a fixed page size and insert order)

interpreter.sourceDelivery: SQL query text + a database image

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The single most promising non-general-purpose entry. SQLite is designed to be embedded with a pluggable VFS: implement a scaffold_env-backed VFS and an amalgamation build against wasm32-freestanding and you have a deterministic query contract. The official build's OPFS VFS is irrelevant here -- you would supply your own.

determinism.notes: Plain scalar C, no EH, no SIMD, no GC. Real determinism work is at the SQL level, not the wasm level: pin the page size, disable random(), fix ROWID assignment and collations, and require ORDER BY (result ordering is otherwise unspecified).

interpreter.sourceDelivery: SQL text + an in-memory database image

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The original (2012) SQLite-in-browser. Entirely in-memory, which is closer to Scaffold's model than the OPFS-backed official build. Superseded by the official build for most uses.

determinism.notes: Same SQL-level caveats as sqlite-wasm.

interpreter.notes: Its value is the pluggable JS-implemented VFS layer -- the first OPFS-backed SQLite. VFS implementations are moving from Asyncify to JSPI.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The most useful reference in this dataset for the transport question: it demonstrates a JS-implemented VFS where every storage call can block, using Asyncify or JSPI -- structurally the same problem Scaffold's JspiTransport solves for blocking host calls.

interpreter.notes: Based on DuckDB v1.5.4; tested in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Node.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Analytical SQL in the browser is genuinely impressive, but the C++ codebase depends on exceptions, and the fast builds want SIMD and threads.

determinism.notes: The 'mvp' build drops EH/SIMD/threads and would be the only candidate; also large, and parallel aggregation ordering is a determinism hazard.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Nesting a wasm interpreter inside a Scaffold contract gives you metering, a smaller trusted feature set, and full control of trap semantics -- at a large constant-factor slowdown. Plain C, small, easy to retarget imports.

Wasmi's lineage is blockchain runtimes (it was the substrate/casper interpreter), so deterministic execution and fuel metering are first-class concerns rather than afterthoughts.

interpreter.artifact: blink.wasm (buildable; the project targets many hosts)

A ~250KB module that runs arbitrary static x86-64 binaries is a remarkable universal-runtime option -- at heavy interpretation cost, and with a large syscall surface you would need to cut down hard.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: The best-established real-world instance of the exact pattern in question: a versioned, content-addressed compiler shipped as a wasm module, producing bytecode for a separately-deployed deterministic interpreter. Worth reading closely for how they handle compiler-version pinning and reproducible output.

implementations.name: EVM interpreters in wasm (revm / yevm / evmone)

interpreter.artifact: revm built for wasm32 (yevm is a newer async-first Rust EVM with an in-browser simulation layer)

rebuildForScaffold.notes: An EVM is a deterministic, metered, state-transition interpreter -- the closest existing analogue to what a Scaffold execution contract is. Rust, so retargeting the state/host interface onto scaffold_env is a trait impl. Even if you never ship it, it is the most direct A/B comparison for the whole design.

determinism.notes: Determinism is the entire point of the EVM spec; gas metering solves the halting problem the same way you will need to.

compiler.sourceDelivery: a wasm module + an init function to run
compiler.outputForm: a new wasm module whose data segments contain the post-initialization heap
compiler.notes: This is the generic mechanism behind 'compiler' in this model: instantiate an interpreter, feed it source S, snapshot, emit a new module with S baked in. Reported 1.35x-6x faster instantiation depending on workload.

rebuildForScaffold.notes: If you want compiler-as-contract for ANY interpreter without writing a compiler, this is the trick: interpreter.wasm + source -> a content-addressed module that is itself a Scaffold contract. Javy and ComponentizeJS both use it. Snapshot output must be byte-deterministic for a given input, which Wizer aims for but you must verify.

determinism.notes: Determinism of the snapshot depends entirely on the init function being deterministic -- no clock, no random, no address-dependent hashing.

implementations.name: Binaryen (wasm-opt) and WABT in wasm -- infrastructure

compiler.artifact: wasm-opt / wat2wasm compiled via Emscripten (binaryen.js, wabt.js)

rebuildForScaffold.notes: Needed if any compiler-contract wants to optimize or assemble its output in-protocol. Note the split: WABT round-trips faithfully with no instruction changes (good for verifiable transforms), Binaryen optimizes (good for size, but every optimization must be deterministic and version-pinned to stay verifiable). Scaffold's own determinism transformer already does raw binary rewriting in Zig, so a third-party dependency may not be wanted here.

determinism.notes: wasm-opt output must be pinned by version -- optimization results change between releases.

crossCuttingNotes.wasmGcIsTheDividingLine: The languages that got best-in-class wasm support in 2024-2026 (Kotlin, Dart, Scala, OCaml, Java-via-TeaVM, Scheme-via-Hoot) all did it via WasmGC, which Scaffold's determinism transformer bans outright. This is the single largest constraint on the usable set. The ban is liftable: WasmGC exposes no addresses, no reference-to-integer conversion, no byte view of a struct, and no finalizers/weak refs/heap introspection (all deferred post-MVP), so the classic GC nondeterminism sources are absent by construction. What remains is resource exhaustion -- allocation failure (no OOM semantics in the spec) and engine-specific static limits that diverge at validation time. Lifting it requires pre-emptive allocation metering against a protocol cost model, which needs the same type-aware pass as re-enabling integer SIMD. Rationale and the argument against are recorded in scripts/wasm-determinism/README.md. All `blocked`/`likely-blocked` verdicts in this file reflect the rules as they stand today.
crossCuttingNotes.browserFeatureBaseline: WasmGC: Chrome 119, Firefox 120, Safari 18.2 (baseline since late 2024). Wasm 3.0 became a W3C standard in Sept 2025 (GC, EH, tail calls, memory64, SIMD). JSPI: unflagged in Chrome 137 (May 2025), behind a flag in Firefox 131+, in Safari Technology Preview with a WebKit implementer assigned; standardized at phase 4 April 2025. Scaffold's JspiTransport is therefore Chrome-only in production today.
crossCuttingNotes.twoStageInTheWild: Four projects already implement the compiler/interpreter split concretely and are worth reading before designing one: Javy dynamic mode (1-16KB bytecode module + 869KB shared QuickJS plugin, two-function ABI), ruby.wasm + wasi-vfs (packs source files into a new self-contained module without rebuilding the interpreter), Wizer (generic snapshot-as-compiler), and solc-js (versioned wasm compiler feeding a separately-specified deterministic interpreter).
crossCuttingNotes.hostBindingsReality: In practice there are three worlds, not five. (1) WASI p1 -- a stable, small, shimmable syscall set; the only one you can realistically reimplement over scaffold_env. (2) Emscripten -- the module is only half the artifact, the generated JS is the other half; porting means rebuilding, not shimming. (3) Everything else (WASIX, WASI p2/components, wasm-bindgen) -- larger or requiring a transpilation step. WASI p2 has no native browser implementation and reaches browsers only via jco transpilation back to core wasm + JS.
crossCuttingNotes.sizeIsTheHiddenConstraint: Per experiments/wasm-limits/results.md, a minimal Zig contract is ~170 bytes and V8 compiled 10,000 unique modules in ~250ms. Against that baseline, Pyodide (~10MB), DuckDB (~35MB), clang (~100MB) and yaegi (~38MB) are in a different universe. QuickJS (1.4MB), MicroPython (0.3MB), SQLite (~1MB), wasm3 (~0.3MB) and Lua (~0.25MB) are the sizes that fit a per-execution instantiation model.
